stories.title: Families of detained Chinese Christians cling to faith in legal limbo
stories.summary: Chinese authorities detained more than 20 members of the unregistered Zion Church, including pastor Wang Cong, accusing them of fraud linked to church offerings. Families remain hopeful and cling to faith despite legal uncertainty and delayed trials, seeing the charges as a denial of their Christian beliefs. The released founding pastor Ezra Jin expressed deep pain over his colleagues' detention and urged detainees to be courageous, highlighting the personal cost of their faith. Clasping her hands together in prayer, four-year-old Huanle tells God she misses her mum, whom she has not seen since Chinese authorities raided their home in 2025 in a crackdown on their unregistered church. Huanle’s mother Wang Cong is a pastor at Zion Church, one of China’s largest “underground” churches where some Christians choose to worship instead of government-regulated ones. Chinese authorities detained more than 20 of Zion’s members last October, including 43-year-old Wang – one of a series of similar recent clampdowns across the country. “My child saw everything, she cried,” said Ren Zhong, Huanle’s father, as he described how seven unidentified officers had entered their home in Beijing that night before he was held down. “She was in her mother’s arms, and they ripped her away.” Wang was taken along with many of her books, and her family have not spoken to her directly since. China’s constitution guarantees citizens religious freedom. However, the ruling Communist Party, which requires its members to be atheist, has historically regarded organised religion with suspicion. It recognises Protestantism and Catholicism as official religions, but practising organisations must register with the government – something many Christians feel yields an unacceptable amount of control over church affairs and teachings.

stories.title: In Singapore, molest, shoplifting and theft in dwelling rise in first half of 2026: police
stories.summary: The number of theft cases in homes jumped by about 25 per cent in the first half of 2026, even as Singapore’s overall physical crime situation remained stable. There were 459 thefts in dwelling cases at residential premises in the first six months of the year, up 25.1 per cent from 367 cases over the same period in 2025, according to the Singapore police’s midyear crime brief for 2026.
